segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We have one more time in Spanish to learn, one more verb time, and that's the point in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The one that usually we would express with "-ed" in English: wanted, walked, or, you know, the irregular versions: ran, ate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is the point in the past. And it's much more random than the other tenses that we looked at. The point in the past is a little bit more messy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But we will find some logic in it, just not the same one that we've been seeing until now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we will practice with hablar for -ar verbs, and with comer for -er/-ir verbs, and we will use these verbs as our hooks that we can look back to when we need to remember one of these endings.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No te lo envié. The word for "still" or "yet", the same word in Spanish, "still" or "yet", is todavía. Todavía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which is actually the combination of todo, here toda in feminine, meaning "all", and vía, like via in English, is a way. So it's "all the way". But, of course, no Spanish speaker hears that when they hear todavía, just like when we say expressions like "as well", we don't think that that's built of "as" and "well".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the words, sometimes the small words we build these bigger words out of in English and in Spanish don't make much sense to us most of the time. But for a learner, it's useful for you to divide a word like todavía because it's long and you might find it difficult to remember, and if you identify that it's toda and vía, even if that doesn't really make any sense with the meaning of "yet" and "still", it's going to help you internalize that vocabulary.
